html:
The days I’ve stayed now outnumber the days I have left. The countdown feels good.

Two days of mahjong in a row, and I have the illusion of living in a drunken dream. Where am I? What am I doing?

Second Aunt, Dad’s sister, had wanted us to come over in the morning, but Mom had a bit of a cold, so I suggested we skip it and take a day off. After breakfast the three of us went for the last bath of the Year of the Rabbit. For lunch we had barbecue, which I hadn’t had in ages. In my childhood memories, barbecue begins around the end of elementary school. Our family was a little better off by then, and we could eat more meat. My cousin and I both loved it, and my uncle, Dad’s older brother, came up with a great idea: buy beef heart. It tasted much like ordinary beef and was cheaper, so we ate to our hearts’ content. The leftover grilled meat was a treat too; it usually became lunch for Grandma and me the next day. We’d eat it while watching reruns of the TV drama Romance in the Rain on CCTV-8.

My parents drank quite a lot at lunch. Since I got back, I’ve noticed that they like drinking more than they used to, and drink more too. Sometimes they have another round before bed. That explains why last year in Hong Kong, after ordering set meals that came with drinks, they still wanted to order a glass of alcohol on the side. I knew they liked a drink; I just hadn’t realized they’d come to like it even more.

I hadn’t wanted to go in the afternoon either, but we had won money yesterday, so not showing up today wouldn’t look good. We took a taxi over and the battle resumed. After a while my cousins came back from visiting their uncle, and my female cousin, my cousin’s wife, Second Aunt and her husband took turns at the table, while my parents and I rotated. We played until after five, when dinner was served. At dinner I sat next to my nephew, my female cousin’s son, and we talked about all sorts of things. He doesn’t say much to the other grown-ups, but he and I seem to click, and he likes talking to me. When we first met in 2013, I held his hand and he chattered away at me. Then, in a blink, it was 2017 and my wedding, and he was in elementary school. Then I came back in September 2017, and that time we spent longer together, nearly two whole days. He knew a lot and was happy to talk, about music, about Jay Chou, the Taiwanese pop star; there didn’t seem to be any generation gap. The next time we met was this year. More than six years have gone by, and he has turned into one of those street-smart “social guys,” with pierced ears and a cigarette dangling from his lips. But when we talk, he’s still the little kid who held my hand in 2013.

My female cousin talked about how she built her business, and her brother told me to write it all down quickly: the entrepreneurial journey of a businesswoman. I said, “How about I come back and work for you?” She said, “You can start by sweeping the floor.” She is grateful to my dad for his help, and she said the whole thing had gone smoothly; many wise and capable people had helped her along the way. A few drinks in, her husband started talking more too: “When she gets impatient, so do I. When she gets sour, I get sour too.” They went through several bottles, and Mom, looking a little anxious, came over to check on them several times.

At last the plates were cleared, and my female cousin went to do the washing up. She is allergic to dish soap and couldn’t find any rubber gloves. Mom hesitated, then said, “Let me do it.” She had washed all of two bowls when the gloves turned up. My cousin’s wife came over grinning and dragged Mom away: “Let her do it, haha.”

Two expressions come to mind for my cousin’s wife: social butterfly, and “smooth on all eight sides,” as the Chinese idiom has it, meaning someone who can handle anyone. With her around, no conversation ever hits the floor. She never gets stage fright, she keeps an eye on everything, she reacts quickly and always strikes the right note. Since my cousin’s business took off, she has stepped back to look after the child and travel full-time. Mom likes her a lot and enjoys talking with her. Who wouldn’t? With her there is never an awkward silence; she has a magical way of putting people at ease. Of everyone I know, she must fit “smooth on all eight sides” best. She doesn’t think much of the Chinese education system either, and wants to send her child to an international school and then abroad. I agreed wholeheartedly and suggested going abroad for the undergraduate degree: high school is too young, grad school too old. The kid sat next to us, bashing away at a video game, lost in a digital world, paying no attention to our conversation or the clatter of mahjong beside us.

We got home after nine. Tomorrow is New Year’s Eve: time to brace for a long day.

The sky over home is a bright, clear sky
